Lottie Moon
LOT-ee MOON
proper noun
Lottie is a familiar form of Charlotte, from the Germanic Karl, “free woman”; her given name was Charlotte Diggs Moon, and the great Southern Baptist missions offering at Christmas bears her name.

Biblical Definition

Charlotte Diggs “Lottie” Moon (1840–1912) was a Southern Baptist missionary to China whose forty years of labor and whose name now grace the Christmas offering by which Southern Baptists fund their foreign mission work. Born to a Virginia plantation family and well educated for her day, she was converted in young womanhood, and after teaching for a season she answered the call to China, going out under the Foreign Mission Board to Tengchow in Shantung province. She gave herself first to schools and then increasingly to direct evangelism among the women of the interior villages, dressing as the Chinese, eating their food, and winning a hearing where foreigners were despised. She wrote letters home that pricked the conscience of the churches, pleading for more laborers and more support, and urging the women of the South to organize for the cause — a summons that helped birth the great missions offering. In the famine and turmoil of her last years she gave away her own food and funds to the starving until her own body failed, and she died at sea on the way home, spent in the service of Christ. She held the gospel to be the one hope of China’s millions and counted no privation too great. She remains a beloved emblem of self-denying obedience to the Great Commission.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Southern Baptist missionary to China for forty years, whose pleas for laborers gave rise to the Christmas missions offering that bears her name.

expand to see more

LOTTIE MOON, a Southern Baptist missionary to China (1840–1912), serving four decades at Tengchow in Shantung.

Educated in Virginia, she gave up a teaching career to carry the gospel to China’s women.

She dressed and ate as the Chinese to win a hearing among people who despised foreigners.

Her letters home roused the churches and helped found the annual Christmas missions offering.

She gave away her own food in famine and died at sea, spent in Christ’s service (2Co 12:15).

Key Scripture

2Co 12:15 — "And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved."

Mat 9:38 — "Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest."

Joh 12:24 — "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Modern Corruption

Moon’s self-denying mission is recast by colonial-guilt revisionism as cultural imperialism, despite her humble identification with the people she served.

expand to see more

The modern colonial-guilt reading treats missionaries like Lottie Moon as agents of Western imposition who exported their culture under the cloak of religion. The charge collapses upon her actual life. Moon laid aside her Western dress, her Western food, and her Western comforts to live as the Chinese among the Chinese, that she might win some (1Co 9:22). She did not come to enrich herself or her nation; she gave away her own bread in famine and died emptied of all. To call such love imperialism is to mistake self-sacrifice for self-aggrandizement and to despise the command that sends preachers to those who have not heard (Rom 10:14).

The lesson to recover is that the corn of wheat must fall into the ground and die if it is to bring forth fruit (Joh 12:24). Moon’s spending of herself is the very pattern of gospel ministry, after the example of the apostle who would gladly spend and be spent for souls. The offering that bears her name still sends laborers into the harvest, and the church honors her best not by apologizing for her calling but by obeying the same Lord of the harvest who sent her forth.

Hebrew Roots

A free woman of the South made herself a servant of all, that she might gain China for Christ.

expand to see more

Lottie — a pet form of Charlotte, from Germanic Karl, “free.”

Moon — an English surname; her name now marks the Christmas missions offering.

The Chinese called her by a local name as they took her for one of their own.

Her plea turned on the noun labourers — “pray the Lord of the harvest” (Mat 9:38).

“Offering” from the Latin offerre, to bring before, names the gift sent in her memory.

Usage

"Each Christmas, Southern Baptists give to the offering that bears Lottie Moon’s name."

"Lottie Moon dressed and lived as the Chinese to gain a hearing for the gospel."

"In her final famine Lottie Moon gave away her own food until she could give no more."
